sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is endemic in Asians and North Africans. Radiologically it is first identified as asymmetry of the Fossa of Rosenmüller (FR) in the nasopharynx, which is also visible on the cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Eighty three consecutive CBCTs including the whole nasopharynx (10 × 10 cm and 10 × 5 cm fields-of-view (FOVs)) of 28 males and 55 females. The CBCTs and the prints of their air-filled pharynxes were reviewed and assigned to one of Takasugi’s 3 types: Type A, no FR; Type B, some FR; and Type C, full and open FR.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The Types A/B/C were 12/11/5 for males and 10/22/23 for females, respectively. Type C was more common in females. Nasopharynx shape on CBCT appeared tadpole-shaped, not cuboidal for the 10 × 10 FOVs, revealing the main difference between medical imaging of the supine patient and dental CBCT of the vertical patient.

sec.title: Discussion and Conclusions
sec.p: The nasopharynx, an important site of malignancies, is prominently displayed on medium-to-large FOV CBCT. The minority of CBCTs which display asymmetry, particularly the Fossa of Rosenmüller, is easily recognised by dentists. To avoid undue referral of false positives, care should also be taken with regard to the clinical history and examination of the neck, especially for lymphadenopathy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Although the nasopharynx is found immediately posterior to the maxilla on conventional radiography (lateral cephalogram, dental panoramic radiograph (DPR) and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT; Figure 1)), most dentists are oblivious to it. Yet it is the seat of very important lesions, such as the nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), which is endemic among East Asians, North Africans and the Inuit.1Fig. 1
Takasugi 3 types of Fossa of Rosenmüller (FoR) (top row) and corresponding axial CBCT reconstructions (bottom row). Type A, shallow or nearly absent FoR; Type B, deep but narrow FoR; Type C, deep but wider FoR.Fig 1 dummy alt text

The nasopharynx is frequently described as a box defined by the base of the skull, the posterior nares and the line between the basion and posterior-nasal-spine (PNS). Arising from each posterolateral aspect of this box is the Fossa of Rosenmüller (FoR), extending through the Sinus of Morgagni above the superior constrictor muscle (Figure 2). The FoR is where the NPC occurs.1 As the contrast resolution of CBCT is generally poor, such pathology is visualised only by the asymmetry of the air-filled pharynx.Fig. 2
Box-shaped, mucosa-lined, air-filled nasopharynxes (in blue) with the Fossa of Rosenmüller emerging from the posterolateral wall as blue wings.Fig 2 dummy alt text

Given that measurements of the otherwise normal nasopharynx and the FoR vary widely,2,3 a better, more clinically applicable system was developed by Takasugi et al.,4 which revealed 3 types of FoR on multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT). When the FoR was almost absent, it was designated Type A; when present but thin, Type B; when present and thick, Type C (Figure 1).

As the human body displays considerable symmetry, both externally and internally (i.e. brain, lungs, etc.),5 such symmetry has been an important clinical feature since time immemorial. Recently, almost 1,000 dental radiation–induced cancers are occurring annually in the United States. Although most are caused by conventional radiography, a substantial number are attributed to CBCT.6 Assuming that each CBCT prescription is clinically indicated, a leading industry safety document has called for the use of the ‘smallest available field of view (FOV) setting that will meet the clinical objective’7 to minimise the dose to the patient. Thus, while focusing on FOVs, in addition to the linear, volumetric and area measurements of earlier studies, this study reviews novel parameters that most clinicians can use more easily, such as the assessment of the symmetry of 3 independent nasopharyngeal triangles.

The objectives of this retrospective CBCT study include identifying the frequency of the 3 Takasugi types; determining the bilateral symmetry of nasopharyngeal structures using 3 triangles (the eustachian tube (ET) triangle, FoR triangle and anterior wall triangle); and quantifying nasopharyngeal volume and surface area.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: Ethical approval for this study was obtained (H24-02158 and H25-00496) to review retrospectively consecutive 86 10 × 10 cm and 189 10 × 5 cm FOV CBCT datasets of the maxilla acquired using a 3-dimensional (3D) Accuitomo Morita machine, made between 1 January 2021 and 13 January 2025. All CBCTs were performed solely for dental purposes. There were no indicators in the dental history or examination to indicate a nasopharyngeal lesion.

The inclusion criteria required the datasets to include the maxilla, because the nasopharynx is immediately adjacent to it. Each dataset had to include the whole nasopharynx. Completeness was determined first by direct inspection of the 3D print. Subsequently, each included dataset was reviewed under standard ambient lighting on an HP Pavilion 32-inch LCD monitor (1280 × 1024 resolution; 300 cd/m²). To ensure consistent orientation for all linear and morphometric measurements, all CBCT datasets were reoriented to a standardised head position prior to analysis. On the axial view, the mid-sagittal plane was adjusted so the nasal septum midline was perpendicular to the horizontal plane, ensuring symmetric visualisation of bilateral landmarks. On the sagittal view, head pitch was standardised by aligning the nasal floor plane parallel to the horizontal plane. Finally, on the coronal view, a midline along the nasal septum was verified to be perpendicular to the horizontal plane to confirm consistent, symmetrical positioning of nasopharyngeal structures across all datasets.

Once the DICOM datasets were imported into CoDiagnostiX, they were printed on a SprintRay Pro95 printer using Die and Model 2 TAN resin. Each model, printed and virtual (Figure 3), was reviewed in 5 standardised orientations (posterior, posterosuperior, superior/directly from above, right and left lateral views).Fig. 3
After confirmation by 3-dimensional (3D) printing (5-image set above) that the dataset completely encompassed the whole nasopharynx for that patient, virtual 3D models (5-image set below) were generated, and the dataset was used for linear measurements and triangular morphology. Ant, anterior; L; left. Lat., lateral; post, posterior; R, right. The lateral reconstruction displays the same ‘tadpole’ shape as seen in the 10 cm × 10 cm FOV datasets.Fig 3 dummy alt text

The measuring protocol integrated elements from previous reports2,3 into a novel triangular framework developed for this study. All measurements were performed on axial slices at the level of the nasal floor and grouped into 3 triangles (Figure 4), then entered into an Excel file for analysis.Fig. 4
Axial CBCT scans at the nasal floor showing eustachian tube (ET) triangle (green), the Fossa of Rosenmüller (FoR) triangle (red) and anterior wall triangle(blue).Fig 4 dummy alt text

The FoR morphology was classified according to the 3 Takasugi types:4 A, B and C (Figure 1). In cases with asymmetry, the appropriate type was assigned separately to each side (e.g. Type A/B, Type A/C or Type B/C). When the Takasugi classification differed between the 2 sides, the more complex side determined the overall Takasugi classification for that dataset: Type B for Type A/B and Type C for Type A/C and Type B/C.
The volume (in cubic millimetres (mm³)) and surface area (in square millimetres (mm²)) of the STL files were calculated using the ‘Analyse’ function in Meshmixer.

Intra-examiner reliability was evaluated for all linear, volumetric and surface area measurements in 9 randomly selected cases (10.8%). Inter-examiner reliability was assessed on the same 9 cases measured independently by the primary examiner and an oral and maxillofacial radiologist. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each parameter.

Statistical analysis used SPSS software (version 29.0), with a significance level of P < .05 for all tests. Differences in linear, volumetric and surface area measurements were assessed using independent-samples t-tests. Takasugi types were evaluated using Pearson correlation coefficients or χ2 or Fisher exact test (FET).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of the 278 (156 males and 122 females) only 83 (28 males and 55 females) imaged the whole nasopharynx, confirmed by printing. Although the majority of the datasets were male, just over 20% of them were included, whereas almost half of the female datasets were included. This sex difference between the included and excluded datasets was significant; χ2 was 24.07 and P < .001. The age range of the 83 datasets was 10-87 years (mean age of 59.44 years; standard deviation (SD) = 17.57). The majority of the scans (78.3%, n = 65) had a 10 × 5 cm FOV while the remaining 21.7% (n = 18) had a 10 × 10 cm FOV. Whereas the 10 × 5 cm FOVs encompassed the maxilla alone with the nasopharynx immediately adjacent to it, displaying its classic box/cube shape, the 10 × 10 cm FOVs of both jaws revealed that the nasopharynx had a ‘tadpole’ shape (Figure 3).

Table 1 summarises the linear measurements taken across specific anatomical landmarks in Figure 4, corresponding to the 3 triangles in the nasopharynx, for male and female participants. Statistically significant differences were observed at 2 anatomical locations: the left ET and the right FoR in females. The coefficient of correlation (r) for the right/left sides of the ET triangle is r = 0.662; P < .001; that of the FoR is r = 0.886; P < .001; and that of the anterior wall is r = 0.926; P < .001. These strong correlations across all regions confirmed the inherent bilateral symmetry of these normal nasopharynxes. Figure 5 reveals that of the 3 triangles, the measurements of the FoR vary most widely, particularly those of the base, joining the most lateral of the right FoR to that of the left. Furthermore, although it varied most, its median is 35 mm, not far from the longest measurement of 48 mm. Half of the samples were within the 35-48 mm range.Table 1
Comparisons of linear measurements based on measurement location and sex. P < .05 is a statistically significant difference.Table 1 dummy alt text

Comparing the values for the Takasugi types (the blue-lined box in Table 2) indicated a significant difference between the sexes (FET; P = .024). Whereas Types A and B appeared across almost all decades in Table 2, Type C was more frequent in females aged 30-79 years. Type A dominated in older males, and males had fewer Type C cases overall, scattered throughout the decades.Table 2
The distribution of Takasugi’s nasopharyngeal types (A, B and C), stratified by sex and age group (in decades).Table 2 dummy alt text
Image, table 2 dummy alt text
Ten of 83 cases (12.0%) showed asymmetric anatomy: 6 Type A/B, 1 Type A/C and 3 Type B/C; 6 occurred in females and 4 in males. This was not a significant FET; P = 0.45.

Nasopharyngeal volume varied, ranging from 1,563.5 to 13,765.2 mm³ (mean = 6,744.4 mm³, SD = 2,148.9). Surface area also varies widely, ranging from 1,272.3 to 10,061.5 mm² (mean = 2,813.5 mm², SD = 1,037.6 mm²). These findings highlight the broad anatomical variation of the nasopharynx in the sample and provide a quantitative reference for future morphometric comparisons. Although males exhibited slightly higher mean values for both volume (6,872.5 mm3, SD = 2326.7 mm³) and surface area (2,933.5 mm², SD = 1545.9 mm²) compared with females (6,679.1 mm3, SD = 2071.8 mm³ and 2,7562.4 mm², SD = 654.7 mm², respectively), the differences were not significant (P = .73 for volume and P = .46 for surface area). These findings suggest that, despite minor numerical differences, nasopharyngeal size and complexity were comparable between the sexes in this sample.

Intra-examiner reliability testing displayed excellent reliability (ICC = 0.898-0.996) for the linear measurements and good reliability for volume and surface area measurements (ICC = 0.772 and 0.874, respectively). There was excellent inter-examiner agreement for nearly all linear measurements (ICC = 0.898-0.999), good agreement for surface area measurements (ICC = 0.843), but only moderate agreement for volume measurements (ICC = 0.634).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Male datasets were significantly excluded because most of them did not include the whole nasopharynx, their heads being too big for the FOV used. Nevertheless, the clinical purpose which prompted the CBCT prescription was successfully fulfilled in every case. This was already revealed in males failure to display the upper neck and, consequently, calcified carotid artery atheromas on DPRs.8 This exclusion of male structures is unlikely to happen when larger FOVs are used.2,3

Even though Epstein-Barr virus tests have been used for nasopharyngeal diagnosis and screening for over a decade, in the absence of control groups they ‘do not provide solid evidence of a benefit associated with screening for nasopharyngeal cancer, especially in nonendemic regions’.9 Therefore, in the meanwhile, clinicians should be aware of other indicators of this cancer. The widespread use of CBCT affords dentists a role in the earlier detection of this important cancer.

The proportions of the 3 types in Takasugi et al.’s MDCT study differed from those in the present CBCT report. Type B was significantly more frequent in Takasugi’s study,4 whereas Type C was most frequent in the present report. This reflects the pharyngeal wall hanging vertically curtain-like from the skull base in vertically positioned CBCT patients, in contrast to it lying flat in MDCT patients, who are supine when the MDCT scan is performed.

Despite the 3 nasopharyngeal triangles’ near-identical means for right and left sides; in Table 1, confirming the nasopharynx’s inherent bilateral symmetry. Furthermore, referring an otherwise normal patient solely because of a radiologically asymmetric FoR (albeit accounting for a minority of cases) can not only overwhelm a service already under pressure but also inflict harm on the patient by performing unnecessary investigations.9 As mentioned earlier, one source of such harm is ionising radiation.6 Therefore, the whole process should begin with the patient’s initial examination, during which the patient’s demographic markers (specifically ethnicity) and accompanying clinical signs, such as recent epitasis, nasal congestion, unilateral neuropathy and/or a hearing defect and cervical lymphadenopathy, are taken into account.1 Clinical examination for cervical lymphadenopathy is particularly valuable in the detection of not only any head and neck cancers but also those arising elsewhere, such as gastric cancer.10

Once the initial examination is completed, the appropriate radiology can be prescribed based on clear clinical indications. If the dentist cannot keep the FOV as small as possible, covering only a part of the jaws,7 then the dentist should ensure the entire dataset has been reviewed by a radiologist, particularly the extra-gnathic areas.

The nasopharyngeal ‘tadpole’ apparent on Figure 3’s lateral views of 10 × 10 cm FOV CBCT underscores the importance of posture in CBCT interpretation and highlights how patient positioning can affect the appearance and evaluation of critical anatomical landmarks such as the FoR, ET and surrounding soft tissue structures. Recognition of this configuration may enhance diagnostic awareness and guide critical review of this often overlooked region.

Although there is considerable interest in CBCT of the pharynx in cases of obstructive sleep apnoea, other pathologies of the nasopharynx do not appear to have earned similar attention. This may be because of poorer inter-examiner reliability of the measurements of the nasopharynx’ volume.11 Although this reflects the moderate inter-examiner reliability of volume measurements in the present study, it does not consider the excellent inter-examiner reliability of its linear measurements. Furthermore, this study’s triangles used for the first time afford the dentist an appreciation of their symmetry, particularly the FoR triangle which is truly symmetrical in the great majority of normal datasets.

Although images taken primarily for diagnosis and detection of diseases such as the orthodontist’s DPR were exceptionally well scrutinised so that all features were identified and noted, a fifth of those taken solely for measurement, such as the lateral cephalogram (LC), had at least 1 undetected incidental finding (IF) that was clinically relevant.12 Therefore, there is a risk that IFs in CBCTs may be likewise overlooked if dentists prescribe and use CBCTs solely for pre-implant planning and do not consider the resultant dataset for routine review for IFs. The use of CBCT in such a way would deprive the patient of timely treatment.

An important limitation of this study was the exclusion of each patient’s ethnicity from the clinical record; as a result, no comment could be made on the significantly larger measurements of the left ET and the right FoR in Table 1. Ethnicity is important because NPC, which was the focus of this study, is endemic in East Asians, North Africans, the Inuit and their diasporas. Even though the inter-examiner reliability for volume measurements in this study was only moderate, the impact of this in the clinical context of a dental office is reduced given that the most important aspect are the apparent asymmetries between the right and left sides of the triangles.

Despite the over 2-decades-long and ubiquitous use of CBCT in dentistry, frequently with large FOVs that image the nasopharynx, little has been done to include it in dental education. This study and a recent editorial1 are important steps towards remedying this.

list-item.p: The nasopharynx is the seat of important lesions, namely the NPCs.

The triangulation method requires only a single axial slice with easily identifiable landmarks, making it efficient, reproducible and less time consuming, allowing dentists and radiologists to assess symmetry and quickly identify deviations that may indicate early NPCs.
While asymmetry in the Fossa of Rosenmüller is an important red flag, attention also should be paid to the routine history taking and clinical examination, including lymphadenopathy.
Because CBCTs of the maxilla made with medium-to-large field of view will include the nasopharynx, this important fact needs to be addressed in all aspects of dental education.
